https://www.surinametimes.com/artikel/sp.text: Engels Spain slams 'selfish' EU response to Ceuta migrants SPAIN - Spain has condemned the "selfish, polarising and unlawful" reaction of some EU countries to the influx of about 60,000 migrants from Morocco to Ceuta. Officials say almost all those who reached the enclave on 30 July have returned, while Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said on Saturday that the death toll had risen to at least 67. It comes after Italy temporarily suspended the EU's border-free Schengen arrangement with Spain, as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called the scenes "shocking". Finland and Denmark backed Italy's move, while Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš urged a temporary suspension of Spain's Schengen membership. In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he had "serious concerns" about some European governments. He said the Spanish government had fully restored control over the border and prevented any "unauthorised onward movement towards continental Europe" in less than 48 hours. While most had shown "support and solidarity", Sanchez said other European governments had chosen to attack Spain, "driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest", and pointed out that Ceuta was not part of the Schengen area. "The European Union cannot afford this kind of selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction," he stated. The Spanish leader called for an urgent meeting with EU interior ministers to "reaffirm that the security of our external borders is a shared responsibility of all Member States". Meanwhile, 22 of the EU's 27 countries also called for emergency talks in an open letter, citing "serious concerns" regarding the developments in Ceuta. https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: Network Rail said this summer’s extreme heat ‘presented exceptional challenges’. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA View image in fullscreen Network Rail said this summer’s extreme heat ‘presented exceptional challenges’. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA Climate crisis Britain’s railway prepares for more extreme weather as intense El Niño develops Experts say more must be done to adapt to changing climate, after two trains derailed within 24 hours during a recent heatwave Priya Bharadia Fri 21 Aug 2026 14.07 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 14.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Railway companies are racing to prepare for another brutal summer next year, as a developing El Niño could see 2027 break more heat-related records. Britain’s railway system has already been under stress from extreme heat this summer, with several operators reducing timetables and train speeds. Two trains derailed within 24 hours during the UK’s fifth heatwave in August, in what Network Rail said had “presented exceptional challenges to the railway”. “Traditionally, our railway system hasn’t been designed for hot weather. So that puts our railway system under stress but also our overhead lines as well. That can also cause trouble for the whole [railway] system, not just the ground infrastructure,” said Xueyu Geng, a professor of ground engineering at the University of Warwick. The Met Office has said that the El Niño event developing over the Pacific Ocean is likely to be the strongest for more than 100 years, with the UK forecast to experience increased rainfall and stormy weather this autumn due to the “unprecedented” weather pattern. In 2024, Network Rail increased their projected five-year spending on climate, earthworks and drainage by five times the amount allocated from 2019. “I believe Network Rail has done a great job to maintain our railway network, but we still need to be able to adapt more in order to cope with this changing climate,” Geng said. She warned Britain must begin to factor in higher temperatures as part of the design standards for its railways. “We need to look at how the hot countries are managing their railway systems. For example, in Spain, their rail system is managing between 0C and 45C. Saudi Arabia is 10C to 55C. The track is pre-stressed. We need to manufacture the pre-stress level in order to cope [with extreme heat].” Geng explained that Britain’s railways can typically handle temperatures as low as -10C, and this will need to be maintained. “We might have extreme cold as well. But, in the meantime, we need to look at the upper boundary temperature, and to actually manufacture our rail to cope with both kinds of extreme temperatures.” Prof Adam Scaife, the Met Office’s head of long-range forecasting, said the scale of the growing El Niño is unprecedented. “We’re expecting the biggest El Niño for over a century, [with Pacific sea temperatures] peaking at something over 3C. That is unheard of in modern climate records.” Rail operators need to be prepared in the coming year for both “potentially prolonged periods of hot dry weather and more intense rainfall and storminess,” said William Powrie, professor of geotechnical engineering at the University of Southampton. “There will need to be a serious look at parts of the network where past decisions have compromised the infrastructure, such as the extensive singling on the Salisbury to Exeter line, and reducing the train speed to account for poor track quality as a result of soil moisture deficit destroys the timetable,” Powrie said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion “The immediate priority should be to use the warning time we have,” said Ioannis Koliousis, associate professor at the Cranfield School of Management. “Before a potentially wetter and stormier autumn and winter, Network Rail should intensify drainage clearance, culvert inspections, earthwork monitoring and vegetation management, particularly at locations with a known history of weather-related failures. “The most important consideration is that we should now distinguish between maintenance and adaptation. Clearing a drain prepares us for the next storm, [but] redesigning or increasing the capacity of that drainage system prepares us for the next 30 years. We need to be doing both.” A spokesperson for Network Rail said: “Our long-range forecast suggests it will be a warm, wet winter – in line with climate change predictions for Britain – and we are doing all we can to be ready for that. Britain’s railway is one of the safest in the world and improving its resilience to more frequent and extreme weather is an ongoing priority. “We are continuing to invest in making the railway more resilient to extreme weather and climate change. This includes a £2.6bn programme of works in track maintenance and renewals, including drainage, earthworks, track and overhead power improvements, as well as monitoring and predictive technologies to identify risks earlier and enable proactive intervention.” Explore more on these topics Climate crisis Network Rail Rail industry Rail transport Transport Travel & leisure El Niño southern oscillation news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/.text: Four people have appeared in court charged with murder after a newborn baby girl, named as Baby S, was found dead with 33 wounds from 15 separate stabbings . At Sheffield Magistrates' Court on Wednesday, September 2, prosecutors told a district judge that the baby’s body was found on top of a washing machine in an outhouse at an address in the Wincobank area of Sheffield , South Yorkshire, on Sunday, August 29. Andrea Skopova, 20, Peter Horvath Jnr, 19, Peter Horvath Snr, 38, and Nina Horvathova, 37, appeared before the court on Wednesday morning charged with the murder of Baby S. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter They were remanded in custody and will appear at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday. Horvath Jnr, Horvath Snr and Horvathova, all of Holywell Heights, and Skopova, of Robey Street, Grimesthorpe, Sheffield, are also charged with causing or allowing the death of a child, and perverting the course of justice by cleaning the scene of the alleged crime. All the defendants are Slovakian nationals, the court heard. A 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named, appeared at the court later in a separate hearing, charged with the same perverting the course of justice offence. The girl sobbed in the dock as representations were made about whether she should be released on bail. District Judge Tim Spruce decided she should be remanded in youth custody until Thursday, when she will appear at crown court with the other defendants. Prosecutor Luke Hopkinson told Mr Spruce that the baby’s mother is the defendant Andrea Skopova. The father is unknown, Mr Hopkinson said. Skopova is the girlfriend of the defendant Horvath Jnr, who is the son of the other two adult defendants. Mr Hopkinson said Horvath Jnr is not believed to be the father. Baby S was found wrapped in a towel and in a blue bag in an outbuilding at an address in Holywell Heights. Mr Hopkinson said she had suffered 33 wounds from 15 “separate stabbings”. A forensic post-mortem has confirmed that the baby’s cause of death as resulting from stab wounds. A number of family members packed into the court for the nine-minute long adult defendants’ hearing, many in tears. The four adults stood wearing identical grey t-shirts and flanked by four security guards. Two women, aged 26 and 37, who were arrested on suspicion of murder remain on bail. Lauren Costello, Deputy Chief Crown Prosecutor at CPS Yorkshire and Humberside, said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute four individuals with murder following a police investigation into the death of a newborn baby girl in the Wincobank area. A fifth individual has been charged with perverting the course of justice. “Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings. “We have worked carefully with South Yorkshire Police as they carried out their investigation. We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendants are active and they have the right to a fair trial. “It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings."

https://www.politico.eu/article/there-ar.text: Russia is holding its first parliamentary elections this weekend since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — a vote that sees the opposition scrambling to give voters options in a field increasingly narrowed by the Kremlin. The shadow of the war looms large over proceedings. As Ukraine intensified strikes on Russian territory and showed greater tolerance for civilian casualties, Russia’s Supreme Court in August barred Yabloko — the country’s only openly anti-war party — from fielding a national list of candidates in the State Duma, Russia’s lower house. And with dissenting voices all but reduced to silence, some opposition figures — including Yulia Navalnaya, widow of Russian opposition leader Alexey Navalny — are asking Russians to vote for candidates who seem at least neutral on the war. Advertisement Advertisement But other opponents of the Kremlin say Navalnaya’s strategy is giving credibility to sham elections that are only held to justify Russian President Vladimir Putin’s maximalist war against Ukraine and tighten his grip on Russian society. “To whoever comes to us with a sword — do not expect mercy,” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in a campaign ad for Putin’s United Russia party, alongside NHL superstar Alex Ovechkin and the propagandist Margarita Simonyan, who runs the state broadcaster RT. Putin’s veterans The Kremlin’s response to the opposition suggests it is worried that people are growing tired of the war. By removing anti-war candidates from the ballot and promoting pro-war voices, Moscow seeks to overstate public support for the invasion of Ukraine, says Ivan Preobrazhensky, a Russian political scientist based in Prague. “By electing them, people are effectively endorsing the policies of the ruling party and the government,” he told POLITICO, even though voters have no real alternative. Yabloko received between 1% and 2% of votes in previous parliamentary elections and was seen as “politically dead” by the Kremlin, according to Maxim Reznik, a former party leader in St. Petersburg. By allowing it to run, Reznik said, the Kremlin “wanted to show that just 1.5% of Russians oppose war.” But reports in Russian media suggested that Yabloko’s recent positioning as “ the only peace party, ” as well as its advocacy for an immediate ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, had boosted its electoral support. The Nezavisimaya Gazeta reported on a July poll from an unnamed agency giving Yabloko a rating of 9.4%. Faridaily, an outlet founded by independent journalist Farida Rustamova, reported that internal government polling put the party around 5.5% . Advertisement Advertisement A month later, the party’s deputy chairman Lev Shlosberg was sentenced to 11 years in prison for “discrediting” Russia’s army, and the party’s registration was canceled by the Supreme Court a month later after bizarre proceedings over alleged copyright violations . Although some Yabloko candidates are allowed to compete in single-member constituencies, the ruling lets pro-war politicians fully retain the overwhelming grip they have on the Duma. “There are no decent parties left,” said Maxim Katz, a former municipal councilor in Moscow’s Shchukino district who later ran campaigns for key opposition figures including Navalny and is now living in exile. “They’re all giving Nazi salutes and telling how great the war is,” he told POLITICO. Ten parties are running lists in the elections, including Putin’s United Russia party, the Communist Party, the nationalist Liberal-Democratic Party, Fair Russia and New People. Members of these five political movements unanimously backed the Kremlin’s annexation of Ukraine’s eastern regions and their inclusion into Russian territory, and have been echoing Moscow’s pro-war rhetoric. In place of Yabloko’s ousted candidates, the Kremlin has promoted its own alternatives. More than a thousand Russian veterans of the war in Ukraine will be running — one of whom, Eduard Shonov , allegedly served in a brigade that occupied the Ukrainian town of Bucha, where Russian forces massacred several hundred civilians at the beginning of the war. For Russians, the war is no longer a distant reality. Recent Ukrainian strikes against Russian cities and infrastructure have caused fuel shortages and made people fearful of attacks. For a large part of the country that agreed to ignore the war as long as it “did not concern them,” the consensus expired “as soon as drones started hitting their cities,” Preobrazhensky said. Advertisement Advertisement ‘Smart voting’ The Russian opposition is still seeking to make its voice heard in an increasingly repressive environment. Navalnaya called the upcoming elections a “propagandistic exercise” for Putin, and believes it is essential to prevent him from getting results that will legitimize his war effort in Russia and in the West. “Our task is to convey to the majority of Russians — the anti-war majority — that, despite total censorship, fear, and repression, these ‘elections’ represent literally the last opportunity to safely express protest against the policies of Putin and his United Russia party,” she told POLITICO. Navalnaya and Katz advocate for what they call “smart voting” — an endorsement strategy to defeat United Russia by backing candidates who are against, or at least less supportive of the war. The strategy was pioneered by Alexey Navalny himself in 2018 after he and his allies were mainly barred from running in presidential and municipal elections. “Smart voting” relies heavily on Yabloko candidates running in single-member districts, but as they are not present in many parts of Russia, some of Navalnaya and Katz’s endorsements include candidates from the Communists and other pro-governmental parties. This approach has been criticized by some members of the Russian opposition, including the head of Yabloko, Nikolay Rybakov. Voting for parties who are already in the Duma amounts to “supporting those who send members of Yabloko to prison,” he said at a meeting with party supporters in St. Petersburg on September 15. Endorsing candidates is “the wrong bet,” Reznik, the former Yabloko official, told POLITICO. “The voting results are in the Kremlin’s hands. They’ll rewrite everything anyway. Just you wait and see.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck05.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead By Azadeh Moshiri South Asia correspondent Published 5 hours ago At the Pashupatinath temple, on the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Madan Lal Lawat joined other families in honouring loved ones who were lost when a deadly flood tore through the China-Nepal border last month. In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead, allowing relatives to perform last rites. With more than 5,000 people still missing and the government ending rescue operations, this is the only way people like Lawat can honour the dead. Five of his relatives - including his brother - were caught in the water's onslaught and are still missing. Lawat survived because he was driving his bus outside his village, Betrawati. The last Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave. "I don't know how to start over. Police say they're still searching for the bodies, but I'm not sure they'll ever be found," Lawat says. He has little doubt they are dead. But legally, their fate is far more complicated. In Nepal, a missing person is only presumed dead after 12 years. Image source, Supplied Image caption, The last Madan Lal Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal (pictured) died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave Section 40 of Nepal's Civil Code does allow for some exceptions, but it does not have a provision for disasters like the flood witnessed last month. Families like Lawat's have told the BBC they are struggling to obtain death certificates, affecting everything from accessing flood compensation to the transfer of properties and even inheritance. Relatives can receive up to 25,000 rupees (Â£122; $162) for funeral costs, in addition to about 200,000 rupees (Â£981; $1,302) in bereavement compensation for the first relative who died, and 100,000 rupees (Â£491; $651) for each additional death. But this is only possible once they submit a death certificate. So as families try to rebuild their lives, many are now caught in an administrative nightmare. "In view of the current disaster, the law is outdated," says constitutional law expert, Bipin Adhikari. He explains the law was meant to account for people who travelled abroad and weren't heard from for years. "But technology has advanced now, it isn't as difficult to send or receive information," he argues. For Lawat, the legal minefield has made an already devastating loss even harder to navigate. When he tried to obtain a death certificate last week, officials at the local municipality office turned him away. "They said they're still discussing the death certificate issue. We aren't sure what to do now. There's so much uncertainty," he tells us. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Most of Betrawati village was swallowed up in the floods Even when bodies are recovered, identifying their identities is a slow and challenging task. More than 1,400 bodies have been recovered so far, and Nepal has little experience in processing DNA at such scale. In some cases, authorities have taken DNA samples, then buried the bodies with markers in the ground, should families claim them. Given the scale of damage and loss, families say compensation is desperately needed. Nepal's latest assessment counts 7,570 private buildings damaged or destroyed, home to nearly 33,000 people based on census data. The BBC visited Lawat's village Betrawati just days after the disaster, once the roads to the district of Rasuwa had been cleared. For days, this area had been cut off from the capital Kathmandu, and struggling with a shortage of basic supplies including petrol. The damage in the village was staggering. The ground was nothing but hardened mud and silt. Footage of the flood showed it had swallowed most of the village in just minutes. There was no sign of its bustling market, the local Uttargaya School was in ruins, the houses swept away, and school buses were turned over. Betrawati straddles flood-devastated Rasuwa and Nuwakot, and is part of the Bidur municipality, where the government estimates more than 3,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. It's the largest amount of any municipality. Local governments are now urging the prime minister's office to figure out a way to resolve the death confirmation issue. "Everything is on hold," Bidur's Mayor, Rajan Shrestha, told the BBC. He said it could take up to 12 years for relatives to access the funds they are entitled to. For one of South Asia's smallest economies, finding money for compensation is a challenge, and the sums on offer are small when compared with the scale of the losses. Image source, Supplied Image caption, More than 5,000 people are still missing after the floods, leaving families stricken with grief The government puts damage to personal belongings alone at Â£123 million ($165 million) across more than 8,300 households. This implies losses of about Â£14,800 ($20,000) on average per household, though this figure is only based on census data and modelling, and doesn't represent the exact cost per family. The financial toll makes the death certificates vital for families trying to recover from the disaster. Shrestha is calling on the federal government to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Until then, he says his hands are tied. "We understand the emotional pain for families who have already performed funeral rituals, but officials must work within legal boundaries to avoid future liabilities." The government has told the BBC it is trying to find a solution. In a statement, the prime minister's office said it was "aware of the difficulties" the law may cause families in "exceptional circumstances, including disasters". The home ministry said the government was taking the issue seriously and was ready to amend the law, if required. The legal hurdles families are facing comes as Nepal faces a steep reconstruction bill, which the government says could cost up to Â£3.6bn ($4.8bn). Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Relatives carry Kush grass effigies for cremation during symbolic funerals held for flood victims still reported missing At the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Balen Shah explained rebuilding the country would require more than 10% of its gross domestic product, an enormous burden on the country's economy. Dozens of public buildings including schools, health clinics and hospitals have been wrecked by the floods. That's in addition to roads, bridges, wastewater treatment plants and hydropower projects. Shah is now pushing for grant-based international support rather than new loans. Nepal is one of the lowest emitters of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet one one of the most vulnerable countries to global warming. "When a climate-driven disaster destroys infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan or a patchwork of small grants," he told a room full of world leaders. This is not the first time Nepal has had to recover after a devastating natural disaster. For Tisum Ghale, the past month has been painfully familiar. He and his family lost their home in an earthquake in 2015, and became displaced for months. They eventually settled in Betrawati. But the place that was once a refuge is where 19 of his relatives were killed in last month's flood, including five of his sisters. He survived because he was doing construction work outside of the village. Once again, he is without a home. "I have lost everything," he said. So far he has received no compensation. He desperately needs the money after his home was washed away and he looks after eight children left behind by his sisters. He is one of the thousands displaced, living across 37 holding centres in northern Nepal. Like Lawati and thousands of other families, Ghale plans on holding a funeral without his loved ones' bodies. He hopes the law will eventually recognise what he already knows: his loved ones will not be coming home. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Bear wanders into California library - video California Black bear breaks into California library to raid snacks and eat jar of honey Bear wandered into Mono county free libraries branch ahead of opening, snacking before wandering new releases Maya Yang Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.04 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A California library on Wednesday had a visitor worthy of a story book on the 100th anniversary of Winnie-the-Pooh : a black bear that wandered inside, reportedly raided the snacks and helped itself to a jar of honey. On Wednesday, a black bear walked into the Mammoth Lakes branch of the Mono county free libraries at about 6.10am, more than four hours ahead of its 10am opening time, the library director, Josef Bopp, told local news outlet KMPH . The outlet reported that the bear raided the staff snack supply, eating peanut butter, peach cups, cookies and a jar of honey. It then wandered through the library, checking out the new releases section and reference desk before making its way back outside on its own. The Mono county office of education on Wednesday issued a statement containing surveillance camera video of the bear strolling through the library, sniffing books, a chair and the ground on the way. “This morning the Mammoth Lakes library had a special visitor before the doors opened for patrons,” the office’s statement said. “We can only assume the new Li-BEAR-ian was looking for a copy of Winnie-the-Pooh, published 100 years ago today!” Bopp also had a reminder for the unexpected visitor, saying : “While we love an enthusiastic patron, and we understand the excitement of the centennial, we do remind patrons – and perhaps more importantly our bears – that snacks are not part of the circulating collection.” Written by AA Milne and illustrated by EH Shepard, Winnie-the-Pooh chronicles the adventures of the eponymous anthropomorphic, honey-loving “bear of very little brain” and his friends in the Hundred Acre Wood, including Piglet, Tigger, Eeyore, Rabbit, Owl, Kanga and Roo. Inspired in part by a teddy bear owned by Milne’s son, Christopher Robin, as well as a real-life black bear named Winnipeg at the London Zoo, the book and three sequels have remained childhood favorites for generations. Many also were introduced to Winnie-the-Pooh and his pals when The Walt Disney Company adapted Milne’s creations for film and television. To celebrate the original Winnie-the-Pooh book’s 100th anniversary, Mono county free libraries encouraged residents to visit any of its seven branches to borrow a copy of Milne’s classic or other bear-themed books. The library system has more than 180,000 physical titles, along with additional online resources. Despite the storybook-like encounter, officials reminded residents that black bears are wild animals and should never be approached or fed. They also urged people to use bear-proof trash containers and keep car doors and windows closed.
